sections.title: A complete journey from discovery to playback
sections.body:
DCP+ is Decentralized Pictures’ streaming platform for films and episodic content. Viewers can discover titles, rent or purchase them, subscribe, and watch advertising-supported content. Behind that familiar experience, card payments, wallet signing, blockchain settlement, and DRM-protected media have to agree on when a viewer can press play.

A single viewing journey crosses the browser, a Next.js server, the Laravel API, Stripe, wallet and blockchain services, and protected media delivery. My work was to make those boundaries function as a coherent client application, from the first catalogue request to a playable entitlement.

I joined the engagement through Lazer Technologies in June 2025. From August onward, I was the sole Lazer engineer responsible for the client applications. Building on the early client foundations, I covered application architecture, product implementation, integrations, technical investigations, connected TV, operational tooling, and release preparation. DCP and ECAD owned the principal backend, blockchain, and infrastructure systems; we worked together where the viewer journey crossed those systems.

sections.title: Building the viewing experience
sections.body:
The product began against an evolving API. Early development used mocks, live API integration followed in August 2025, and a larger catalogue arrived in September. As the content and contracts changed, the application needed a stable way to represent what viewers could discover, own, and watch.

I used generated OpenAPI types and a view-model layer to separate API contracts from component contracts. Type generation made backend changes visible during development; mapping code translated endpoint-specific shapes into the models the interface needed. This let me adapt integrations without repeatedly restructuring the presentation layer.

That foundation supported catalogue browsing, collections, search, film and series details, authentication, profiles, and account and device management. My Stuff brought bookmarks, purchases, rentals, and Continue Watching together. Watch progress and resume connected one viewing session to the next, while English and Spanish localization and responsive layouts carried the experience across desktop and mobile browsers.

Episodic viewing extended the model beyond standalone films. The later TV Series work connected browse collections, series and episode details, shared production cards, and admin curation, with purchase targets for a series, season, or individual episode. The important design problem was keeping discovery, ownership, and playback consistent as the content model expanded.

sections.title: Designing around route and session boundaries
sections.body:
The earlier application relied on global providers for responsibilities that did not belong to every route. Request initialization could occur in an unpredictable order, session dependencies were difficult to untangle, and content could flash before an access redirect. Starting work globally also made it harder to avoid requests that an individual experience did not need.

In December 2025, I restructured session orchestration around explicit route boundaries. Instead of asking a single provider tree to prepare every possible journey, each boundary owned the session requirements, authorization, and data readiness relevant to the routes beneath it.

This gave initialization a clearer order and reduced coupling between unrelated experiences. It also made later session investigations easier: there was an identifiable place to decide whether an operation belonged to application infrastructure, authentication, the streaming session, or the current page.

The Next.js backend-for-frontend subsequently moved session tokens into HttpOnly cookies with CSRF protection. It also became the integration point for signed viewer-IP headers on server requests, where the API would otherwise see the hosting platform’s address. ECAD designed the signing and verification scheme; I implemented the client and BFF integration, including fresh signatures on retries.
items: Root infrastructure supplied the application-wide foundation without owning every route’s session work.
Authentication routes owned entry into the viewer session.
The main streaming boundary coordinated the session needed for the viewing application.
Page-local boundaries owned the data and permissions required by their particular experience.

sections.title: Separating viewer identity from wallet connectivity
sections.body:
Wallet signing helped establish the viewer session, so wallet connectivity and application authentication had become coupled. That dependency was too broad. A wallet is needed to sign certain operations, but it should not have to remain connected while someone browses a catalogue or watches a film.

Unexpected sign-outs initially appeared to be a reconnection problem. Targeted telemetry showed restoration failures while the wallet SDK was still connecting. Rather than adding more aggressive reconnection, I investigated whether wallet restoration should control an already authenticated viewer session at all. DCP confirmed that the initial signature establishes the session and that continuous wallet connectivity is unnecessary for viewing.

I made the viewer session the authority for application authentication and treated the wallet as an on-demand signing capability. Wallet restoration could then fail without automatically ending the viewer’s session, while purchase, subscription, and renewal operations could request signing when they needed it.

The development traces supported that boundary. Before the change, nine of eleven restore-failure events coincided with sign-out in the same trace and second. Afterward, seven failures across six traces had no sign-out in those traces. This small internal testing sample validated the direction of the change; it was not a measure of production retention.

sections.title: Engineering commerce across multiple systems
sections.body:
Buying a title was an asynchronous workflow across independently owned services. A Stripe payment could finish before blockchain settlement, and settlement could finish before the application could see a playable entitlement. Treating any one of those events as “purchase complete” risked showing a stale call to action or leaving a viewer staring at an indefinite pending indicator.

I consolidated five separate sources of client settlement state into one transaction state machine. The unified model made progress explicit, including a longer-than-usual state, and gave the interface a consistent account of where the transaction stood. Payment completion, settlement, and playable access remained distinct. A dedicated backend transaction-status contract was still a useful next step, but the client no longer had to assemble its story from competing state sources.

The commerce work covered rentals and purchases, Stripe and TALNT payments, wallet signing, and subscription checkout and renewal. A saved-card prototype helped shape the payment APIs developed by ECAD. From there, I built payment-method setup and card management, reusable payment methods, and a feature-flagged one-click checkout implementation based on an approved RFC.

Interrupted signing needed to be recoverable within the operation. I designed in-place recovery so a wallet problem could be handled during a purchase or subscription rather than forcing the viewer to abandon the workflow. Later subscription work added renewal controls, payment-method changes, and clearer errors.

Cross-system diagnosis was as important as the state model. One apparent signature failure turned out to be a blockchain-service failure reported as InvalidSignature. Request traces and reproducible checks helped give the owning team a precise failure to investigate. For saved cards and off-session renewal, test-mode Stripe checks were more useful than relying on remembered provider semantics. The result was a clearer client workflow and better integration evidence, not a claim that the client could eliminate every external settlement failure.

sections.title: Protected playback across browsers and devices
sections.body:
PRESTOplay replaced an earlier Shaka playback path. I integrated it with DRMtoday, FairPlay, and Widevine across HLS and DASH delivery, then built the surrounding viewing behavior: custom controls, subtitle and audio selection, profile preferences, progress events, resume, and error reporting. Later work added intro, recap, and credits markers, mobile fullscreen improvements, and concurrent-session recovery.

The Safari investigation exposed why a working player integration was not enough. After the migration, Chrome could play protected content while Safari could not. Safari’s native HLS path did not carry the authorization headers the delivery path expected. Alternate playback paths could not solve FairPlay decryption, playlist tokens did not propagate as required, and cross-site cookies were being dropped.

Working with DCP’s engineering lead, I traced the problem across the player, browser, and media-delivery boundary. CloudFront signed cookies, a CDN alias on the application’s site, and appropriate CORS configuration established a functioning Safari path by April 30, 2026, ahead of the May beta. A later iOS regression after a CDN configuration change reinforced that media authorization had to be revalidated when delivery settings changed.

The October release package included a subsequent iOS 17.1 and later path using Managed Media Source, enabling authorization injection with FairPlay support. That provided another compatibility path rather than making the earlier same-site CDN arrangement the only option. It was accompanied by consolidated player UI and updated iPhone controls and layout.

Playback recovery also became a product interaction. The Watch Here work let a viewer reclaim playback after another session took over. It was included in the October release package, alongside the compatibility work, with device testing and production verification remaining part of rollout.

sections.title: Shared client architecture and connected TV
sections.body:
I worked across a shared TypeScript core and the platform-specific applications. Generated API clients, view models, session and authentication logic, shared streaming behavior, and error handling gave web and TV a common foundation. Catalogue and commerce interactions could reuse those contracts without requiring identical interfaces.

The Samsung Tizen application brought the viewing journey to a device with different sign-in, navigation, and release constraints. Device sign-in and remote navigation needed a TV-specific experience around the shared logic. Keeping those concerns separate helped the applications share behavior without making the web interface dictate the television interface.

A signed Samsung build passed Seller Office pre-testing on June 5, 2026. That was a concrete distribution milestone, with business inputs, final validation, and submission completion still needed for a store launch. The Expo/React Native application reached a TestFlight walkthrough before priorities shifted toward web; it was not a launched native product. LG webOS remained an opportunity requiring implementation and device testing.

sections.title: Advertising and operational tooling
sections.body:
Advertising had to fit the viewing experience even when inventory was unavailable. After an earlier AWS MediaTailor proof of concept, DCP selected Indicue. I implemented the VAST integration, ad-break scheduling, and client rules included in the October release package. Empty inventory and failed ad requests could fail softly so the film continued, and content-gap rules counted from ad pods that actually started.

An independent AVOD validation harness made real VAST requests without requiring an eligible ad-supported title in the catalogue. That gave product and QA a way to investigate behavior while content and vendor dependencies were still being resolved. Admin collection curation also gave authorized staff a self-service way to publish collections, select productions, and edit membership.

Localization exposed a different operational boundary. Publishing resources had required a manual admin import and administrative authentication, while replacement imports could overwrite keys belonging to other platforms. I implemented a CI-scoped Laravel import endpoint with token middleware and feature tests, then a GitHub Actions workflow that uploaded changed locale resources to the environment associated with the target branch.

The workflow used merge-safe updates, key-level diffs, and missing-translation diagnostics. Uploads were deterministic; an early agent-assisted PR-comment path was later replaced with a deterministic script as well. A scoped CI service token authenticated publishing, separate from the GitHub token used for comments. The workflow was exercised in development and staging and removed a recurring manual step from those environments.

These tools were part of making the application maintainable after delivery. Generated contracts, shared error catalogues, CI test gates, playback harnesses, architecture notes, and release documentation helped turn integration knowledge into artifacts another engineer could use.

sections.title: Delivery and milestones
sections.body:
The clearest evidence of the engagement is the journey that became possible: discover a title, obtain access, and watch protected content. The milestones below mark that progression across the participating teams.

I closed the engagement by preparing the v0.3.0 release package on October 2, 2026, following the final client demo on October 1. Technical release notes, a stakeholder summary, and the changelog documented the work since the July production release. The package included TV Series, Indicue advertising, subscription management, wallet/session isolation, unified settlement, and Watch Here recovery. At handoff, completed deployment and production validation of that package were not confirmed; API rollout, feature flags, and separate TV releases still governed availability.
items: March 16, 2026: A real purchase settled on-chain and became playable through joint work with DCP and ECAD.
April 30, 2026: Safari DRM playback was working.
May 8 and May 15, 2026: The web service went live, followed by the Cannes beta.
June 5, 2026: A signed Samsung build passed Seller Office pre-testing.
October 2, 2026: v0.3.0 release package and technical handoff prepared.

sections.title: What the engagement reinforced
sections.body:
The most important shift for me was learning to follow the complete product journey rather than stopping at the application boundary. Safari playback, wallet restoration, and purchasing only became understandable when I could trace what each independently owned system expected and give its owner a precise problem to resolve.

Clear boundaries made that work easier. Routes owned their session responsibilities, viewer identity stopped depending on continuous wallet connectivity, and transactions acquired an explicit state model. Real integrations and targeted telemetry were what tested those decisions. On another engagement of this breadth, I would establish the shared end-to-end validation path earlier and keep it alongside the architecture and release documentation, so the next engineer inherits both the implementation and a way to verify it.
